477.title: A field in wartime (Jeremiah 32:6–15)
477.hook: with the enemy at the gates, Jeremiah buys land: houses will be bought here again
477.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Jeremiah 32 in times of crisis as a picture of hope that acts, and preachers have used it in wartime, in economic downturns and when churches build or plant in struggling neighborhoods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new covenant, and your line was on the heart. Did your words stay with you? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

A real estate agent calls during a war. The enemy army is camped around your city. Siege ramps are going up against the walls. Food is running out. Everyone knows how this ends. And the agent says: there's a field for sale, just outside town. Actually, it's behind enemy lines right now. Interested? It sounds like a joke. Jeremiah said yes. He was under arrest at the time, held in the guard's courtyard of the king's palace, because he'd been saying out loud that Babylon would win. And his cousin came to see him with exactly that offer. Today, a purchase made under siege.
screen: `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `JEREMIAH UNDER ARREST.` → `A FIELD FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: It's the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem. Jeremiah's cousin Hanameel comes and says: buy my field at Anathoth, our home village; the right to redeem it is yours. In Israel's law, when family land was about to be lost, a close relative had the right, and the duty, to buy it back so it stayed in the family. And God had told Jeremiah this visit was coming. So Jeremiah does it, and he does it properly. He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs the deed. He calls witnesses. He makes two copies, one sealed and one open, and hands them to his scribe, Baruch. Then he tells Baruch to put both in a clay jar, so they'll last a long time. Why the clay jar? Because he isn't buying for this year. He's buying for after. And then he says why, in the King James Bible: "For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." This is the same prophet who has been warning for years that the city will fall. He hasn't changed his message. He still says the city will fall. But he puts his money on the far side of the fall. And the next thing he does is pray, and in the prayer he admits it seems absurd: the city is being handed to the Chaldeans, and you told me to buy a field. He begins with: "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." Hope, here, isn't a feeling. It's a signed deed in a clay jar.
screen: `THE ARMY AT THE WALLS.` · `THE RIGHT TO REDEEM IS YOURS.` · `SEVENTEEN SHEKELS, A DEED, A JAR.` · `HOPE AS A SIGNED DEED.` · then, large: `FIELDS SHALL BE POSSESSED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one hopeful investment. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your world that feels besieged: your health, your town, a relationship, the news. Don't pretend it's fine. Jeremiah didn't. Then ask: what small thing could I put on the far side of this? A tree you could plant. A garden bed for next spring. A class you could sign up for. A letter to your future self. A friendship you could invest in. Picture yourself signing the deed. If you pray, you can offer that hope to God, the way Jeremiah did. The bell holds the time.
A field in wartime. Jeremiah's purchase under siege: seventeen shekels and a sealed deed in a clay jar, a bet on the far side of the fall.
Your line: houses will be bought again. Today, make one hopeful investment, small and concrete, in a future you can't see yet. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

478.title: Dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
478.hook: a valley of bones rattles together, and breath comes into them
478.howItsDone: Ezekiel 37 is read at the Easter Vigil and at Pentecost in many churches, and has long been sung and preached in African American churches as a vision of hope; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on the Sabbath during Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a field in wartime, and your line was houses will be bought again. What hopeful investment did you make? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Jeremiah stayed in Jerusalem. Another prophet, Ezekiel, a priest, was among the exiles already taken to Babylon, living by a river there. And his visions are strange and vast: wheels full of eyes, a scroll he's told to eat, a Temple measured out cubit by cubit. Then the news reaches the exiles: Jerusalem has fallen. The Temple is gone. And the people say something that may sound familiar to anyone who's been through a long loss. Our bones are dried up. Our hope is lost. We're cut off. It's over. Into that, Ezekiel is carried by the spirit and set down in a valley. Today, what was in the valley.
screen: `EZEKIEL AMONG THE EXILES.` → `JERUSALEM HAS FALLEN.` → `OUR HOPE IS LOST.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones." He's led around them. Very many, and very dry. Not recent. Long dead. And God asks a question: "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel's answer is careful, almost wise: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." He doesn't say yes. He doesn't say no. Then God tells him to prophesy to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD." So he does, and there's a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to his bone. Sinews, then flesh, then skin. But there's no breath in them. Bodies, lying there. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, this time to the breath: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain. And breath comes into them, and they live, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. Now the word that holds the vision together. The Hebrew word ruach appears all through this passage, and it means breath, and wind, and spirit, all at once. The spirit carries Ezekiel. The breath enters the bodies. The four winds supply it. It's one word, and English needs three. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say our hope is lost. I will open your graves and bring you home. Jewish communities read this vision on the Sabbath during Passover, the festival of freedom. Christians also hear in it the hope of resurrection, and of the Spirit who gives life.
screen: `A VALLEY FULL OF DRY BONES.` · `O LORD GOD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `BODIES, BUT NO BREATH.` · `RUACH: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT.` · then, large: `CAN THESE BONES LIVE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe toward something stalled. Settle, and breathe deeply. Feel the air come in. Notice that you didn't make it; it arrived. Then bring to mind something in your life that feels like dry bones: a project, a hope, a friendship, a faith that's gone quiet. Picture it lying there. Ask Ezekiel's question honestly: can this live? Don't force an answer. Then, with each breath in, picture breath moving toward it, and with each breath out, release your need to control it. If you pray, you can say: thou knowest. The bell holds the time.
Dry bones. Ezekiel's valley of the long dead, joined bone to bone and filled with breath: a picture of a people's hope coming back to life.
Your line: can these bones live? Today, take one stalled thing and do one small act of breath: one email, one page, one call, one prayer. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
479.hook: I will take out the heart of stone
479.howItsDone: Christians often pray Ezekiel 36:26 when asking God to change them, and it is read at the Easter Vigil, at confirmations and at services of renewal; it appears in many hymns and worship songs about the Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the valley of dry bones, and your line was can these bones live? What stalled thing got a breath? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Stone doesn't feel anything. That's what makes it good for walls. A sibling, an old friend, a parent, a coworker: someone hurts a person enough times, and something in that person goes hard. The name pops up on a phone, and there's nothing, or worse, a kind of cold click. It works like protection, and sometimes it is. But walls have a way of spreading: harder with one person, then a little harder with everyone. Ezekiel had a word for that. He'd watched a whole people grow hard: hard toward God, hard toward the poor, hard toward the truth. Today, a promise about the heart.
screen: `A NAME POPS UP.` → `A COLD CLICK.` → `THE HARDNESS SPREADS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, God says through Ezekiel: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." First, the heart. In the Hebrew Bible, the heart, lev, isn't mainly where you feel. It's often where people think, decide and choose. Your whole inner self. So a heart of stone isn't just sadness. It's a self that can't be moved, can't be taught, can't respond. And a heart of flesh is one that's alive again: soft enough to feel, to change, to care. Notice the trade isn't weak for strong. It's stone for flesh. Flesh can be hurt. That's the point. Only something that can be hurt can also love. Now look back a few chapters. Earlier in the same book, in chapter eighteen, Ezekiel tells the people: make you a new heart and a new spirit. Make it yourselves. And here in thirty-six, God says: I will give you a new heart. So which is it? The book holds both. Some readers put it this way: the new heart is something you're called to reach for, and something you can only receive. Christians often connect this verse to the work of the Holy Spirit, and Jewish readers hear in it God's promise to renew Israel after exile. Both hear the same image: stone, taken out; flesh, given back.
screen: `A NEW HEART WILL I GIVE YOU.` · `LEV: WHERE YOU THINK AND CHOOSE.` · `ONLY FLESH CAN BE HURT, OR LOVE.` · `MAKE IT, OR RECEIVE IT? BOTH.` · then, large: `AN HEART OF FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften toward one person, just a little. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've gone hard toward. Not the person who hurt you most; start smaller. Picture their face. Notice the stone: the tight chest, the set jaw, the ready list of what they did. Don't throw the list away. Just set it down for a minute. Then try to see one ordinary, human thing about them: they get tired, they were a child once, someone they love is sick. Let your chest loosen by one degree. If you pray, you can ask for a heart of flesh. The bell holds the time.
A heart of flesh. Ezekiel's promise: a hard, stony self taken out, and a living heart put in, soft enough to feel and to love.
Your line: a heart of flesh. Today, soften toward one person by one degree: a kinder word, a reply you'd usually skip, or simply not adding to the list. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

480.title: The fiery furnace (Daniel 3)
480.hook: three young men won't bow, and a fourth walks in the fire with them
480.howItsDone: The story of the three young men is a favorite in Sunday schools, and in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican worship their song from the furnace, the Benedicite, is sung or said as a canticle; Orthodox Christians sing it in the Christmas season and at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stone heart and the new one, and your line was a heart of flesh. Who did you soften toward? Day four hundred eighty.

A golden statue stands on a plain outside Babylon, sixty cubits high, ninety feet or so, gleaming in the sun. King Nebuchadnezzar has gathered every official in his empire: governors, judges, treasurers, all of them. A herald shouts the rule. When the music starts, horns, pipes, harps, every kind of instrument, everyone falls down and worships the statue. Anyone who doesn't goes into a burning furnace. The music starts. Thousands of people drop to the ground at once. And three young men, Jewish exiles who've risen to high posts in Babylon, stay standing. Their names in Babylon are Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Today, the fire.
screen: `A GOLDEN STATUE ON A PLAIN.` → `WHEN THE MUSIC STARTS, BOW.` → `THREE MEN STAY STANDING.`

segments.voice: They're hauled before the king, furious, who gives them one more chance. And their answer, in the King James Bible, is one of the bravest speeches anywhere in scripture: "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods." Listen to the hinge: but if not. They believe God can save them. They don't claim to know that he will. And their choice doesn't depend on the outcome. They won't bow either way. The king, enraged, has the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. So hot that the soldiers who throw the three men in are killed by the flames. And then Nebuchadnezzar leaps up, astonished: "Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God." Four. Loose. Walking. When they come out, not a hair is singed, their clothes are untouched, and, the text says, the smell of fire had not passed on them. Who is the fourth? The king himself says God sent his angel. In the original Aramaic he says the fourth looks like a son of the gods, which is how a Babylonian king might describe a heavenly being. Many Christians, from early on, have seen in the fourth figure the Son of God, Christ, present before his birth; others see an angel, as the king says. Either way, the heart of it is the same: they weren't kept out of the fire. Someone walked in it with them. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also include the long song the three men sing in the flames.
screen: `BUT IF NOT.` · `SEVEN TIMES HOTTER.` · `FOUR MEN, LOOSE, WALKING.` · `NOT KEPT OUT, BUT ACCOMPANIED.` · then, large: `THE FORM OF THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small thing you won't bow to. Settle, and breathe. Think of a pressure in your life that asks you to go along: a joke at someone's expense, a shortcut that isn't honest, a crowd that expects you to drop to the ground when the music starts. Pick something small. Picture yourself standing, quietly, without drama. Notice the fear that comes with it. Then picture not being alone in it. If you pray, you can ask for courage, and for company in the fire. The bell holds the time.
Bar elahin. Aramaic for a son of the gods, how the king described the fourth figure walking in the flames with three young men who wouldn't bow.
Your line: a fourth in the fire. Today, stand firm on one small thing, kindly and quietly, and remember: being in the fire doesn't mean being alone in it. Day four hundred eighty.

481.title: The lions' den (Daniel 6)
481.hook: Daniel prays at his window three times a day, law or no law
481.howItsDone: Some Christians keep fixed times of daily prayer, morning, midday and evening, through the Liturgy of the Hours, the Angelus, the Book of Common Prayer offices or simple personal habit; Jewish tradition prays three daily services, facing Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fiery furnace, and your line was a fourth in the fire. What small thing did you stand firm on? Day four hundred eighty-one.

The lions' den often gets told as a young hero's story, all muscles and courage. Follow the book's own timeline instead. Daniel was carried off to Babylon as a youth. Now Babylon itself has fallen, and a new ruler, Darius, sits on the throne. He has outlasted the kings who took him. He's spent a lifetime in government, so honest and capable that Darius plans to set him over the whole kingdom. And the other officials can't stand it. They look for corruption and find none. Finally they say, we'll never catch him unless it's about the law of his God. Today, the trap they set.
screen: `NOT A YOUNG HERO.` → `AN OLD, HONEST OFFICIAL.` → `NO CORRUPTION TO FIND.` → `A TRAP ABOUT HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: They go to the king with flattery: make a decree that for thirty days, no one may pray to any god or person except you, O king. Break it, and you go to the lions. Darius signs it, and by the law of the Medes and Persians it can't be changed. Now watch Daniel. In the King James Bible: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." As he did aforetime. That's the quiet center of the story. Daniel doesn't stage a protest. He doesn't close the shutters and pray in secret either. He just keeps doing what he's always done, at the window that faces a city he hasn't seen since he was young. The habit was already there; the law simply found it. Three times a day echoes a psalm: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Jewish tradition keeps three daily times of prayer, and synagogues traditionally face toward Jerusalem. The officials catch him, of course. The king, who has set his heart on saving Daniel, tries until sundown to find a way out and can't. Daniel goes into the den, and a stone seals the mouth. The king spends the night fasting and sleepless. At dawn he runs to the den and calls out: is thy God able to deliver thee from the lions? And from inside: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." Christian readers often hear this story as a call to steady, daily faithfulness, the kind that's ready before the test comes.
screen: `A DECREE: PRAY ONLY TO THE KING.` · `AS HE DID AFORETIME.` · `THE WINDOW FACING JERUSALEM.` · `THE LIONS' MOUTHS SHUT.` · then, large: `THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set three times for today. Settle, and breathe. Picture your day: morning, the middle, evening. Choose three moments you could pause, even for thirty seconds. After breakfast. At lunch. Before sleep. Picture a window in each one, a place you could turn your face toward. Then, right now, take the first pause: be still, breathe, give thanks for one thing. If you pray, you can pray as Daniel did, with thanks. If not, simply stop and notice. The bell holds the time.
The lions' den. Where Daniel was thrown for praying at his open window, three times a day, as he always had, and the lions' mouths were shut.
Your line: the window stays open. Today, pause at the same three times, morning, noon and night, and keep the habit, even when it's inconvenient. Day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: I taught Ephraim to walk (Hosea 11:1–4)
482.hook: God as a parent holding a toddler's hands, bending down to feed
482.howItsDone: Christians read Hosea 11 in sermons and Bible study as a picture of God's parental love, and Matthew 2:15 quotes its first verse in the story of Jesus' childhood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lions' den: Daniel kept praying at his open window three times a day, law or no law. Your line was the window stays open. Did you keep one small appointment with what matters? Day four hundred eighty-two.

Watch a parent teach a toddler to walk. They crouch behind the child, one finger in each tiny fist, and shuffle forward bent nearly double. Their back aches. The child has no idea anyone is holding on. The child thinks they are walking all by themselves, and that's the point. Later, at the table, the same parent leans down with a spoon, patient, while half of it ends up on the floor. Somebody probably held each of us like that once, and nobody remembers it. An old prophet named Hosea reached for exactly this picture to describe God. Not a king on a throne. A parent on their knees in the hallway.

Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel, and in his book the north is often called Ephraim, the name of one of its tribes. Chapter eleven opens like a family album. In the King James Bible: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." The Exodus, remembered not as a battle but as a parent calling a child home. Then the toddler scene: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them." That's the ache in the chapter. The child was held, fed and healed, and never noticed. Verse four keeps going: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love." Not chains for an animal. Human cords, the kind a person uses to guide someone they love. And then a farmer's picture: God as the one who eases the yoke off their jaws and bends down to lay food before them. The chapter isn't sweet all the way through. Hosea also names the people's turning away, and the hard years coming. But a few verses later God says, in effect, my heart is turned within me; I can't give you up. The love outlasts the anger. Matthew's Gospel later borrows the first line, out of Egypt have I called my son, and hears it in the story of the child Jesus and his family in Egypt. Christians who follow Matthew hear Hosea on two levels at once: Israel's story, and a pattern that Jesus walks again. Either way, the picture stays. God, in this book, is the one on their knees.
screen: `OUT OF EGYPT: A PARENT CALLING HOME.`
`CORDS OF A MAN, BANDS OF LOVE.`
then, large: `I TAUGHT EPHRAIM ALSO TO GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for a small one. Settle, and breathe. First, remember. Bring to mind someone who held you up before you could stand: a parent, a grandparent, an older cousin, a teacher. You may not remember the moment. Hosea's point is that you probably wouldn't. Just picture their hands. Then think of a small one in your life now: a child, a pet, a seedling on the windowsill, a younger colleague finding their feet. Choose one small act of care you can give them today. If you pray, you can give thanks for the hands that held you. If you don't, simply let the gratitude sit. The bell holds the time.
Ahavah. Hebrew for love, the cords Hosea says God used to draw a people like a parent bent over a toddler, holding their arms, feeding them, healing them unseen.
Your line: cords of love. Today, guide someone small the way Hosea pictures it: gently, from behind, without needing them to notice it was you. Day four hundred eighty-two.

483.title: Your old men shall dream (Joel 2:28–29)
483.hook: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; Peter quoted it at Pentecost
483.howItsDone: Some churches read Joel 2:28–29 near Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, where Peter quotes it; churches that keep the Christian year celebrate Pentecost seven weeks after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea's parent on their knees: I taught Ephraim to walk. Your line was cords of love. Did you guide someone small without needing the credit? Day four hundred eighty-three.

Nine in the morning in Jerusalem, a festival crowd in the streets, and a commotion. A small group of Jesus's followers are pouring out of a house, talking in languages they never learned, and visitors from many nations hear their own home tongues. Some people are amazed. Others laugh: they're drunk. Then Peter, a fisherman who not long before had denied he even knew Jesus, stands up. He says, more or less, it's too early in the day for that. And instead of explaining it himself, he quotes an old prophet, from a book so short it's easy to flip past. The prophet is Joel.
screen: `NINE IN THE MORNING, A FESTIVAL CROWD.`

segments.voice: Joel is only three or four chapters long, and nobody is sure exactly when he lived. His book opens with a disaster: a plague of locusts that strips the land bare. He calls the people to fast and to turn back to God, and then the promises come, first of rain and harvest, and then something bigger. In the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." Look at who is on that list. Sons and daughters, not just sons. Old and young. And the next verse goes further: "And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit." Servants. In earlier stories of the Hebrew Bible, the spirit comes on particular people: a judge like Gideon, a king like Saul, a prophet. Joel pictures it soaked into everyone, the way rain soaks a field after the locusts. Old people dreaming is not a small detail either. It means nobody has aged out of hearing from God. Then the scene in Acts chapter two. Peter tells the crowd, in the King James wording: "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." Christians remember that day as Pentecost, and some call it the birthday of the church. Jews read Joel too, and hear his promise in their own way, as a hope for Israel's renewal. For Christians, Peter's sermon made Joel's list the guest list of the church. And look back at this week: a field bought in wartime, dry bones, a heart of flesh, a furnace, a lions' den, a parent teaching a child to walk, and now the spirit on everyone. Over and over, the prophets refuse to give up on people.
screen: then, large: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone old and someone young. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the oldest person you know and the youngest person you know. Picture each of their faces. Ask yourself: when did I last really listen to either of them, without fixing or correcting? What might the old one still be dreaming? What might the young one be seeing that you've stopped seeing? Just hold them both for a moment. If you pray, you can pray Joel's promise over them in its own words. If you don't, simply decide which one you'll call or sit with this week. The bell holds the time.
Your old men shall dream. Joel's promise that the spirit of God would pour out on everyone, young and old, women and men, servants too.
screen: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: on all flesh. Today, ask one older person what they still hope for, and one younger person what they see coming. Then just listen. Day four hundred eighty-three, and another week on the path.
